theory.title: CI/CD Concepts
theory.content:
Continuous Integration (CI)

CI is the practice of automatically building and testing code on every commit. The goal is to detect integration issues early, keeping the main branch always in a working state.

  • Every push triggers an automated pipeline
  • Tests must pass before code is merged
  • Short feedback loop — developers know within minutes if something broke

Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment

Continuous Delivery: every successful build is packaged and ready to deploy to production. Release is a manual, intentional decision.

Continuous Deployment: every successful build is automatically deployed to production with no human approval. Requires high test coverage and confidence.

/* Pipeline stages */
Commit → Build → Unit Tests → Integration Tests → Staging Deploy → [Manual Approval] → Prod Deploy

/* CD (Delivery) — gate at [Manual Approval] */
/* CD (Deployment) — no gate, auto-deploys */

Why CI/CD Matters

  • Reduces risk — small, frequent releases are easier to debug
  • Faster delivery — automated gates replace manual QA bottlenecks
  • Consistent environments — same pipeline runs in every environment
  • Early bug detection — problems found in CI are 10x cheaper to fix than in production

theory.title: GitHub Actions
theory.content:
Workflow Structure

A workflow is a YAML file placed in .github/workflows/. It is triggered by events and contains jobs.

name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'
          cache: 'npm'
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build

Jobs & Dependencies

Jobs run in parallel by default. Use needs to create a sequential dependency:

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [ ... ]
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [ ... ]
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: [lint, test]     # runs only after both pass
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    steps: [ ... ]

Secrets & Environment Variables

# In workflow
env:
  NODE_ENV: production
  API_URL: ${{ vars.API_URL }}          # repository variable (not secret)
  DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.DB_URL }}  # encrypted secret

# Set secrets: GitHub Repo → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions

Caching Dependencies

- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.npm
    key: ${{ runner.os }}-node-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
    restore-keys: |
      ${{ runner.os }}-node-

theory.title: Deployment Strategies
theory.content:
Blue-Green Deployment

Maintain two identical production environments: blue (live) and green (staging). Deploy to green, run smoke tests, then switch the load balancer. Rollback is instant — just switch back.

  • Zero downtime, instant rollback
  • Requires double the infrastructure cost
  • Database migrations must be backward-compatible during the switch

Canary Deployment

Route a small percentage of real traffic (e.g., 5%) to the new version. Monitor error rates and performance. Gradually increase traffic if healthy.

/* Nginx example: 5% canary */
upstream backend {
  server app-v2 weight=5;   /* canary: 5% */
  server app-v1 weight=95;  /* stable: 95% */
}
  • Real user validation with limited blast radius
  • Requires feature parity for both versions during rollout
  • Ideal for high-traffic apps where full blue-green is too risky

Rolling Deployment

Replace instances one by one. At any moment some instances run v1 and some run v2. Used by default in Kubernetes (RollingUpdate strategy).

/* Kubernetes RollingUpdate */
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    maxSurge: 1        # spin up 1 extra pod before killing old
    maxUnavailable: 0  # never go below desired replica count

Feature Flags

Deploy code to all users but control who sees it. Decouple deployment from release. Allows A/B testing and gradual rollout by user segment.

theory.title: Docker in CI/CD
theory.content:
Why Docker in CI/CD?

Docker packages the application and all its dependencies into an immutable image. The exact same image is built once and promoted through dev → staging → production, eliminating environment drift.

Writing an Efficient Dockerfile

FROM node:20-alpine AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Build stage
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# Production stage — minimal image
FROM node:20-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]

Multi-Stage Build Benefits

  • Final image contains only runtime code — no dev dependencies or source files
  • Smaller attack surface and faster image pulls
  • Build tools (TypeScript compiler, etc.) don't end up in production

Docker in GitHub Actions

- name: Build and push image
  uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
  with:
    push: true
    tags: ghcr.io/org/app:${{ github.sha }}
    cache-from: type=gha
    cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

Container Registries

  • GitHub Container Registry (GHCR) — integrated with GitHub Actions
  • AWS ECR — for AWS deployments
  • Docker Hub — public images and small teams

theory.title: Environment Management
theory.content:
Environment Types

A healthy delivery pipeline promotes the same artifact through multiple environments:

  • Local — developer's machine; fastest iteration, mocked external services
  • CI — automated test runner; ephemeral, clean on every run
  • Staging — production mirror; real external services, internal traffic only
  • Production — live; real users, monitored

Managing Secrets Safely

# .env.example — COMMITTED (template, no real values)
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@host/db
JWT_SECRET=change-me
REDIS_URL=redis://localhost:6379

# .env — NOT committed (.gitignore)
DATABASE_URL=postgres://prod-user:real-pass@prod-host/app

# In CI: inject via platform secrets
# GitHub Actions: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}
# Vercel: project environment variables
# Kubernetes: Secrets mounted as env or volumes

12-Factor App Principles

  • Config belongs in the environment, not the code
  • Never commit secrets to version control
  • Each environment should be as similar to production as possible
  • Treat backing services (DB, cache) as attached resources via URL

theory.title: Pipeline Optimization
theory.content:
Run Fast Checks First (Fail Fast)

Structure your pipeline so the cheapest, fastest checks run before expensive ones. A linting failure should not waste 5 minutes on a full test suite.

jobs:
  lint-and-types:          # 30 seconds
    steps:
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run typecheck
  unit-tests:             # 2 minutes
    needs: lint-and-types
    steps:
      - run: npm test
  e2e:                    # 10 minutes
    needs: unit-tests
    steps:
      - run: npx playwright test

Parallelise Independent Jobs

jobs:
  lint:     { runs-on: ubuntu-latest, steps: [...] }
  typecheck: { runs-on: ubuntu-latest, steps: [...] }
  test:     { runs-on: ubuntu-latest, steps: [...] }
  # All three run simultaneously — total time = slowest job

Caching & Artifact Reuse

  • Cache node_modules keyed on package-lock.json hash — saves 30-60s per run
  • Cache Docker build layers with type=gha
  • Upload build artifacts between jobs with actions/upload-artifact

Path Filtering

on:
  push:
    paths:
      - 'src/**'
      - 'package*.json'
# Skip CI entirely for docs/ or README changes

theory.title: Monitoring & Observability
theory.content:
Three Pillars of Observability

A production system is observable when you can understand its internal state from external outputs. The three pillars are metrics, logs, and traces.

Metrics

Numeric measurements aggregated over time. Used for alerting and dashboards.

  • Golden Signals: Latency, Traffic (req/s), Errors (error rate), Saturation (CPU/memory)
  • Tools: Prometheus (collection), Grafana (dashboards), Datadog, CloudWatch

Logs

Timestamped records of discrete events. Use structured logging (JSON) for machine-parseable output.

// Structured JSON log (Pino, Winston)
logger.info({
  event: 'user.login',
  userId: user.id,
  ip: req.ip,
  duration: 42,
});
// → { "level":"info", "event":"user.login", "userId":"123", ... }

Distributed Tracing

Traces follow a request as it flows across multiple services, identifying latency bottlenecks. Each operation is a span; all spans from one request form a trace.

  • Tools: Jaeger, Zipkin, OpenTelemetry (standard instrumentation API)

Alerting Best Practices

  • Alert on symptoms (error rate > 1%) not causes (CPU > 80%)
  • Set meaningful thresholds — alert fatigue kills on-call rotations
  • Every alert should have a clear remediation runbook
